eviction.title: You got an eviction notice
eviction.subject: eviction
eviction.intro: A notice is a document, not a done deal. What matters now is the date on it, the deadline it starts, and the record you keep from this moment.
now_steps: Keep the notice itself — every page, and the envelope if it came by mail.
Write down the date you received it and how it was delivered — posted on the door, handed to you, or mailed.
Photograph or scan the notice so you have a copy that can't be lost.
Find the deadline on the notice. Minnesota eviction deadlines are short — count from the day you got it, not the day it was written.
Before you respond to the landlord, get the notice in front of a tenant advocate or legal aid office.

repairs.title: Your landlord won't fix something
repairs.subject: repair
repairs.intro: Repair disputes are won on the paper trail: what was broken, when you reported it, and what happened next. Start that trail now, while the details are fresh.
now_steps: Write a dated list of what is broken and when each problem started.
Photograph or video each problem — include something that shows the date.
Put the repair request in writing — text or email counts — and keep a copy.
Keep every reply from the landlord. If they don't reply, note the date you asked and the silence.
Look up the repair obligations that apply where you live before withholding rent or paying for repairs yourself — those steps have rules.

deposit.title: Your deposit is being withheld
deposit.subject: deposit
deposit.intro: Deposit disputes come down to records: what the unit looked like, what the law required the landlord to send you, and when. Gather yours while it's easy to find.
now_steps: Find your move-in photos, the move-in checklist, and your lease.
Keep the deposit statement or itemization the landlord sent — or write down that none arrived, and when it was due.
Write down your move-out date and the day you returned the keys.
Keep every message about the deposit, including any promises made in person — write those down too.
Check the deadline your state gives landlords to return or itemize a deposit — missing it can change what they owe.

retaliation.button: I'm being punished for speaking up
retaliation.title: You think you're being punished for speaking up
retaliation.subject: retaliation
retaliation.intro: Retaliation is about sequence: what you did, and what the landlord did right after. The timeline is the evidence — build it carefully and let the dates speak.
now_steps: Write down what you did — asked for a repair, reported a problem, joined with other tenants — with the date.
Write down what changed after — a rent increase, a notice, threats, a sudden rule — with the date.
Put the two lists side by side. In Minnesota, an adverse action soon after a protected one can be presumed retaliatory.
Save every message from before and after. The tone change is part of the record.
Keep doing everything you're required to do — pay rent on time, follow the lease — so the record stays clean on your side.

entry.button: My landlord came in without notice
entry.title: Your landlord entered without notice
entry.subject: lease
entry.intro: Landlords generally can't enter whenever they want — notice rules live in your lease and your state's law. Each unannounced entry is a fact worth recording the same day.
now_steps: Write down the date, the time, and how you know they were there — you saw them, a neighbor did, things were moved.
Note anyone who witnessed it or any camera that may have caught it.
Save any message where they mentioned coming by — before or after.
Check the entry clause in your lease so you can compare what it says to what happened.
If they left a note or notice, keep it — even a bad-faith notice is evidence.

harassment.button: My landlord is harassing or threatening me
harassment.title: Your landlord is harassing or threatening you
harassment.subject: safety
harassment.intro: Two things matter at once: your safety right now, and the record of every incident. Handle the first one first — help lines exist for exactly this.
now_steps: If you feel unsafe right now, treat that as the emergency it is — contact local help before anything on this page.
Save every message — texts, emails, voicemails, letters. Don't delete the upsetting ones; they are the record.
Write down each incident the day it happens: date, time, what was said or done, who saw it.
Keep a log of unannounced visits and drive-bys — patterns only show when every instance is recorded.
Tell someone you trust what's happening, so you're not carrying it alone.

rent.title: Your rent is being raised
rent.subject: rent
rent.intro: A rent increase has rules around it — notice periods, lease terms, and sometimes local limits. Check the notice against the rules before deciding what it means.
now_steps: Keep the increase notice and write down the date you received it.
Check your lease — is the increase inside a fixed term, or at renewal? Leases usually control when rent can change.
Find the notice period your lease and state require, and count whether they gave it.
Save every message about the increase, including anything said in person — write those down with dates.
If the increase follows a repair request or complaint, note that sequence — it can matter.
